In the shared flat in Aarhus, the group was in a foul mood after the presentation went badly. “It was Daniel's slides,” said Freja. “The chart was wrong.” “And he talked too fast,” added Mads. Even Sofie agreed. Daniel sat with his tea, quiet.

Anders had been listening. It was strange how eager they were. Nobody had mentioned that the group had not rehearsed once. Nobody had mentioned the two evenings they skipped for the football match.

“Can I ask something?” Anders said. “If the slides were fine, what would we be talking about right now?” Freja opened her mouth, then shrugged. Mads laughed, a little embarrassed.

“We didn't practise,” Sofie said slowly. Daniel lifted his head for the first time.

qa.q: What did Freja say was wrong on the slides?
qa.a: Freja said the chart was wrong.

qa.q: What does the group's eagerness to blame Daniel suggest to Anders?
qa.a: It suggests to Anders that the group was avoiding something uncomfortable, namely that nobody had rehearsed.

qa.q: What did Anders ask, and why did the mood change?
qa.a: Anders asked what they would be talking about if the slides were fine, which made the group face the missed rehearsals.

qa.q: How might Daniel have felt when the group finally said they hadn't practised?
qa.a: Daniel probably felt relieved and a little vindicated, since the blame that sat on Daniel alone had at last been shared.

grounding: A thoughtful peer notices a group unusually keen to blame one person and asks what the group is avoiding, and the mood shifts.

The committee room of the cultural club was tense. The sponsor had pulled out, and the treasurer slapped the table. “Aditi was supposed to follow up. It's her fault.” Aditi, a first-year volunteer, went pale. Two members nodded. The secretary said, “Let's just record it as her mistake.”

Abhinav, sitting by the window, felt something off. Everyone wanted this over very quickly. He raised his hand. “Before we write that, can I ask what we were each doing in the three weeks before?”

A silence followed. The treasurer looked at the minutes. “The sponsor's deadline was on the agenda twice,” said someone. “Nobody assigned it.”

The secretary put down the pen. “Then it wasn't only Aditi.”

qa.a: Aditi, a first-year volunteer, was blamed.

qa.a: Abhinav felt uneasy and suspicious because everyone wanted the matter closed very quickly by blaming one new volunteer, which hinted at something they wanted to avoid.

qa.a: Abhinav asked what each person was doing in the three weeks before, which revealed that nobody had been assigned the sponsor's deadline.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Aditi to hear the room turn from blame to shared responsibility?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt huge relief and surprise, but also lingering hurt from having been blamed so fast by people on the same team.

grounding: A thoughtful peer notices a committee's haste to blame one person and asks what it is avoiding, shifting the mood toward shared responsibility.

You asked about my internship? Okay. I'm Nilesh, and the one moment I'm proud of was a question.
Our demo for the client crashed. In the meeting afterwards, the whole team piled on Nitin, the youngest. “Nitin pushed the code.” “Nitin didn't test it.” The manager nodded along. It was almost a relief in the room, like we'd found the answer.
I remembered we'd all agreed to skip testing to meet the deadline. All of us. The manager too.
So I asked, quietly, “If it's all Nitin, what are we not talking about?”
Silence. Then someone said, “The deadline.” And someone else, “We skipped testing together.”
Nitin looked up for the first time. The meeting became about fixing the process, not him.

I was in the student council room that evening, so I saw what Vijay did, though I can't say for sure what he was thinking.
The fest fund was short by a few thousand. Within minutes, everyone was saying it must be Mridul, the treasurer. “He's so disorganised.” “He probably lost it.” People seemed almost excited.
Vijay had been quiet the whole time, watching. Then he asked, in a normal voice, “Why are we so quick on this? Didn't we all spend without receipts this year?”
The room went still. The president looked at the floor.
Someone started going through the receipts box. By ten, they had found most of the missing amount, spent by several of us on snacks and decorations. Mridul went home without being blamed.
